===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:swappen|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|swappen|t=to swap}}, originally meaning "to hurl" or "to strike", the word alludes to striking hands together when making an exchange; probably from {{inh|en|ang|*swappian}}, a secondary form of {{inh|en|ang|swāpan||to swoop}}. Cognate with {{cog|de|schwappen||to slosh, slop}}. Compare also {{noncog|enm|swippen|t=to strike, hit}}, from {{noncog|ang|swipian|t=to scourge, strike, beat, lash}}, {{noncog|non|svipa|t=to swoop, flash, whip, look after, look around}}. More at {{m|en|swipe}}.

{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[exchange#Verb|exchange]] or [[give]] (something) in an non-normal exchange (for something else).
#: {{synonyms|en|exchange|switch|trade}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To [[hit#Verb|hit]], to [[strike#Verb|strike]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1954|author=C. S. Lewis|title=The Horse and His Boy
|passage="Maybe Apes will grow honest, Sister," said Edmund. "But, by the Lion, if he breaks it again, it may be in such time and place that any of us could '''swap''' off his head in clean battle."}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To [[beat#Verb|beat]] the [[air#Noun|air]], or [[ply#Verb|ply]] the [[wing#Noun|wings]], with a [[sweeping#Adjective|sweeping]] [[motion]] or [[noise]]; to [[flap#Verb|flap]].
# {{lb|en|intransitive|obsolete}} To [[descend]] or [[fall#Verb|fall]]; to [[rush#Verb|rush]] [[hastily]] or [[violently]].

* Unlike many determiners, but like many adjectives, {{m|en||much}} is frequently modified by intensifying adverbs, as in “too much”, “very much”, “so much”, and so on. (The same is true of {{m|en||many}}.)

====Usage notes====
* As a verb post-modifier in affirmative contexts, {{m|en||much}} must in standard English be modified by another adverb: ''I like fish '''very much''''', ''I like fish '''so much''''', etc. but not *''I like fish '''much'''''. Adverbial ''much'' can, however, appear affirmatively before certain verbs: ''I '''much''' prefer fish to meat'', ''I '''much''' appreciate your kindness''.
* As a comparative intensifier, ''[[many]]'' can be used instead of ''much'' if it modifies the comparative form of ''many'', i.e. ''more'' with a [[countable]] noun: '''''many''' more people'' but '''''much''' more snow''.
* May be used in humorous questions to draw attention to somebody's undesirable behaviour: "desperate much?", "cherry-picking much?", etc.
